entry.title: Three quick checks before you expect AI search to quote your page
entry.summary:
I've been building small Claude/Cursor skills that review pages for AI-search readiness. Running them on public pages kept turning up the same three gaps. You can check all three yourself in about ten minutes with curl and view-source. You don't need a tool. curl -s https://yoursite.com/robots.txt | grep -iE 'gptbot|claudebot|perplexitybot|google-extended|ccbot'
No output means you have no AI-specific rules, so these bots follow your User-agent: * group. That's fine if it's on purpose. The problems I see are leftovers: a blanket Disallow someone added years ago, or a CDN/WAF bot rule that blocks crawlers the robots.txt says are allowed. Check both. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://yoursite.com/llms.txt

entry.title: I built 35+ PDF tools that never upload your files (Rust + WebAssembly)
entry.summary: Most online PDF tools work the same way: you upload your file, a server processes it, and you download the result. That's fine for a flyer. It's less fine for a contract, a bank statement, or a medical report. I wanted to know how far you can get with no server at all. The answer turned out to be: almost all the way. The result is InBrowserPDF, a set of 38 PDF tools where every file is processed entirely on your own device. Rust compiled to WebAssembly does the heavy work: parsing, merging, compressing, and encrypting. Web Workers run that code off the main thread, so the page stays buttery responsive while a multi-megabyte file is being crunched. The file never leaves the tab. entry.title: Obfuscating a Dapper data-access layer without breaking column-to-property mapping
entry.summary: A micro-ORM like Dapper earns its speed by doing very little magic, but the one piece of magic it does keep is the piece that collides with obfuscation. When you write connection.Query<Customer>("SELECT Id, FullName, Email FROM Customers"), Dapper executes the command, walks the result set, and for each row builds a Customer by matching each column name in the reader to a public member on Customer whose name matches, ignoring case. That match is done by string comparison against the member's name at runtime. Rename Customer.FullName to a with an obfuscator and the FullName column has nothing to bind to — so Dapper leaves the property at its default and moves on. No exception. No log line. Just a Customer whose FullName is null. That silence is what makes this worth a careful post. A broken…

entry.title: Wiring the Keyright SDK into ASP.NET Core DI as a typed HttpClient with resilience
entry.summary: Most Keyright integrations start the same way: someone needs to validate a license against the self-hosted issuing service, so they write new HttpClient(), point it at the ServiceUrl, and ship it. It works in development and on the demo. Then it goes to production and one of two things happens. Either the client is created per call — a fresh HttpClient inside the method that checks the license — and under real traffic the process runs out of sockets. Each disposed client leaves connections in TIME_WAIT, the ephemeral port range fills, and you start seeing SocketException: Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted. entry.title: 10 PCB faults that pass DRC and still cause a respin
entry.summary: Your PCB passed DRC with zero errors. The Gerbers look clean in the viewer. So the board is ready for fab, right? Not quite. DRC checks the rules you gave the tool. It has no idea what the board is meant to do. In design reviews we keep finding the same small group of faults on boards that passed every automated check. Each one is cheap to fix on screen and expensive to fix after the boards come back. Here are ten of them, with the quick check that catches each one. A regulator, an LDO or a MOSFET can come in fixed and adjustable versions, or in two packages, under nearly the same part number. The schematic symbol is drawn for one variant and the BOM orders the other. DRC can't see it because the footprint is fine.
